subtype: Road and vehicle safety in India [Actor]
passage: At the fair on the hill road, Ojas's friends pulled up on one motorbike, three of them squeezed on, no helmets. "Hop on!" one shouted. Ojas looked at the space and at the bend beyond. His stomach felt like a stone. "I'll take the bus," he said. They laughed. "It comes in an hour!" "That's okay." He sat on the bench by the stop, watching the bike go. His sister Bhavna, already at the fair, spotted him when the bus finally came. "You took the bus?" "Yes." Later the three friends walked in with torn shirts and scraped elbows, the bike skidded on gravel, but no one broken. Ojas said nothing.

qa.q: How many friends were on the motorbike?
qa.a: Three friends were squeezed on one motorbike.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he looked at the space on the bike and the bend beyond?
qa.a: Ojas was uneasy and afraid, as if his stomach felt like a stone.

qa.q: What made Ojas's choice hard, and what did it show?
qa.a: Riding three on a bike without helmets felt normal to his friends, so choosing to wait for the bus alone took courage against the crowd.

qa.q: What might Bhavna think when she hears Ojas took the bus?
qa.a: Bhavna probably feels a little surprised and relieved that her brother did not go with the friends who later arrived with scrapes.

grounding: Shows a teenager declining a ride with three on a motorbike and no helmets when local habit made it feel normal.

subtype: Road and vehicle safety in India [Actor]
passage: In their small town near Sangli, Jatin, sixteen, was going to the weekly market with his friends. They had one scooter and no helmets. "Hop on, three of us fit," said his friend. His older sister Minakshi, standing at the gate, said nothing, just looked at him. Jatin hesitated. Every boy in the town rode like this. Nobody wore helmets for the market. But last month, a boy from the next lane had fallen off on the same road. Jatin felt his face grow hot. "You two go. I'll cycle." They laughed and called him a coward. He pedalled after them, sweating. At the market, Minakshi's words later were simple: "That took guts."

qa.q: Where were Jatin and his friends going?
qa.a: To the weekly market.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he said he would cycle?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face growing hot, but also determined, remembering the boy who had fallen.

qa.q: Why was Jatin's choice difficult, and why was it right?
qa.a: Everyone in town rode three on a scooter without helmets, so refusing meant being mocked, but it kept him safe.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see her brother's choice?
qa.a: Minakshi sees it as brave, telling him that it took guts.

grounding: Shows a teenager refusing to ride three on a scooter without a helmet when everyone around does, choosing safety over approval.

subtype: Road and vehicle safety in India [Actor]
passage: Javier and Jana, sixteen and fifteen, flew from Madrid to Goa to spend the summer with their grandmother, who had moved there years ago. On the first evening, their new friends offered them a ride to the beach on a scooter. Three to a scooter, no helmets. "Everyone does it here," one boy said. At home in Madrid, Javier would never have got on a scooter without a helmet. Here, it suddenly felt normal. He almost climbed on. Jana grabbed his arm. "Would you do this at home?" "No." "Then why here?" Javier felt the others watching. "We'll walk," he said. The next day, their grandmother bought two helmets from the market.

qa.q: Where did Javier and Jana fly from?
qa.a: From Madrid.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling as he almost climbed on?
qa.a: He felt the pull of fitting in, as the local habit made the danger suddenly seem normal.

qa.q: What question helped Javier choose safely?
qa.a: Jana asked whether he would do this at home, which showed that only the crowd's habit made it feel safe.

qa.q: How might the new friends see Javier's decision to walk?
qa.a: They might think it odd or overcautious, since riding three to a scooter without helmets is normal for them.

grounding: Shows a teenager in India almost riding three to a scooter without a helmet because everyone does, until a sibling's question helps him choose safely.

subtype: Road and vehicle safety in India [Actor]
passage: After Saturday practice at the district football club, Kishore's friends crowded round one scooter in the club car park. Rohit started it, Faizan climbed on behind, and they both looked at Kishore. "Come on, squeeze in. It's two kilometres." Nobody had a helmet. Half the car park rode like this; the watchman didn't even look up. Kishore's hand was already on the seat. Then he pictured the flyover and the trucks. "I'll take the bus," he said. Faizan rolled his eyes. "Seriously? You sound like my mother." Rohit snapped, "We waited for you, yaar." Kishore's face burned, but he stepped back. Coach Elizabeth, locking the kit room, had heard. "Kishore, I'm going your way. Front seat's free." In the car he stared out of the window, still embarrassed. A few minutes later they passed the scooter, wobbling round a pothole with three heads and no helmets.

qa.q: Who was locking the kit room?
qa.a: Coach Elizabeth.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after saying he'd take the bus?
qa.a: He was embarrassed, his face burning at the teasing, even though he stood by his choice.

qa.q: What made Kishore's choice take courage?
qa.a: Riding three to a scooter without helmets looked normal to everyone, so saying no meant being mocked by friends who were annoyed they had waited.

qa.q: How did Rohit and Faizan see Kishore's refusal?
qa.a: They saw it as fussy and a letdown, rolling their eyes and snapping, because the risk felt ordinary to them.

grounding: Shows a teenager tempted to ride three to a scooter without a helmet because everyone does, and choosing safety against the crowd.
